title: The Recova and the Avenue: the First Intendente of Buenos Aires
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Cisplatine Birth and the Father's Legation (1822-1852)

stops.name: Montevideo: the fifth son of the deposed Director
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish article gives 21 April 1822, the English article 12 April 1822; the contradiction is left standing and the Spanish date is used for placement. The coordinate is Montevideo centro, not Ciudad Vieja
stops.campa: In Montevideo, capital of the province the crown of Brazil now calls the Cisplatina, a fifth son is born to General Carlos María de Alvear and Carmen de la Quintanilla. The father is a man out of office: Director Supremo of the United Provinces in 1815, thrown down within three months and proscribed, living where the Republic he helped make cannot reach him. The child is named Torcuato Antonio. The city he will one day remake is at this moment a town of low houses, cobbles that stop at the edge of the built blocks, and one arcaded market across its main square.
suggested_refs: Montevideo under the Provincia Cisplatina, 1817-1828

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Fuerte and the Plaza de la Victoria: the family restored
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The father's 1822 rehabilitation is attested; no source places the infant Torcuato in Buenos Aires, and the month here is a placeholder within the year of that restoration
stops.campa: The year of the birth is the year the father's rank and property are given back to him, seven years of proscription closed with a stroke of the pen. The household crosses the river to Buenos Aires, to the quarter of the old Fuerte, where a colonial recova of arcaded shops runs across the middle of the main square and divides it into two. No document places the infant Torcuato in these streets; that the family moved with the restored general is the ordinary reconstruction. The recova standing at the centre of the square is not a reconstruction at all. Sixty-one years later he will order it down.
suggested_refs: The Fuerte de Buenos Aires and the Recova Vieja, standing in 1822

stops.name: Washington: the father's fifteen years at the legation
stops.date_confidence: attested for the father: the mission runs 30 June 1837 to 3 November 1852, after an earlier and much shorter mission of 1823-1824. Whether Torcuato was ever in Washington is attested by nothing, and this stop is a reconstruction of the family's possible movement only
stops.campa: From the middle of 1837 the father holds the legation of the Argentine Confederation to the United States, a posting he keeps fifteen years, to his death. Whether the boy and then the young man Torcuato crossed north with him, or stayed in Buenos Aires, no biography consulted will say: every search for a life of him returns an empty page or a dead server. He is fifteen when the mission opens and thirty when it closes. Across those fifteen years the record holds his name and nothing to attach it to, in a family whose head is abroad.
suggested_refs: The Argentine legation to the United States, 1837-1852

stops.name: New York: the death of the founder
stops.date_confidence: attested for the father's death. Torcuato's presence or absence is recorded nowhere and is not asserted here in either direction
stops.campa: Carlos María de Alvear dies in New York, still minister, thirty-seven years after he stood at the head of the Republic and was thrown out of it. The requiem is sung at Old St. Patrick's on Mulberry Street. The body waits decades for its passage home. Torcuato is thirty years old, and no source says whether he was at the bedside, at sea, or reading the news in Buenos Aires weeks after the fact. What the father leaves him is a name that opens every door in the city, and a promise of return that the family will keep in marble, in a vault neither of them has yet built.
suggested_refs: Old St. Patrick's Cathedral, Mulberry Street, New York

segments.name: The Marriage and the Unrecorded Years (1854-1880)

stops.name: Buenos Aires: marriage to Elvira Pacheco
stops.date_confidence: year attested; neither the day nor the church is given by any source consulted, and the month and day are defaulted to January 1. The city is inferred, not stated
stops.campa: He marries Elvira Pacheco y Reinoso, daughter of General Ángel Pacheco, the federal commander who broke the unitarian columns and then withdrew from the wars. The match ties the house of the deposed Director to the house of a general of the other side; in a city that still counts its dead by faction, such a marriage is a treaty. How many children follow, the sources cannot agree: one account names ten, another gives seven of whom three die in infancy and four grow up. Both accounts agree on the names of the four who live, and on the one who becomes president.
suggested_refs: The Pacheco family papers and the descent of General Ángel Pacheco

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Perú y Victoria: the Club del Progreso
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The club's second seat, the Palacio Muñoa at Perú and Victoria, is attested for 1857-1900; Torcuato's own membership is confirmed by no reachable source, and repeated searches for a biography returned 404s. The year marks the opening of that seat, not any act of his
stops.campa: The Club del Progreso keeps its rooms in the Palacio Muñoa at the corner of Perú and Victoria: the place where the men who govern Buenos Aires dine, play cards, and settle in an afternoon what the newspapers will argue over for a month. Its founding president, in 1852, is Diego de Alvear, Torcuato's own brother. No membership list reachable today comes down to Torcuato's name, and every attempt to find one ends in an error page. That he passed through those rooms is inference; it is inference with his brother's chair at the head of the table.
suggested_refs: Club del Progreso, Palacio Muñoa, Perú y Victoria, seat of 1857-1900

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Barrio Norte: the birth of Marcelo Torcuato
stops.date_confidence: attested for the birth. The address of the family residence is nowhere recorded; the coordinate is the Barrio Norte ground associated with the family in this period and is a reconstruction of the location only
stops.campa: A son is born and named Marcelo Torcuato. By the account that counts seven children, three die small and four grow: Carmen, Ángel, Carlos, and this one. The boy will be president of Argentina from 1922, in a country where his father is remembered chiefly as a plaza and a monument. The house is not recorded by number. The family's ground in these years is the Barrio Norte, up the slope toward the Franciscan convent of the Recoleta and the burial field beside it, which at this date has no wall, no paved street, and no gate worth the name.
suggested_refs: Marcelo Torcuato de Alvear, president of Argentina 1922-1928

stops.name: Buenos Aires: twenty-six years the record does not hold
stops.date_confidence: no event is being dated. The stop marks a documented absence running from the 1854 marriage to the 1880 appointment; the year is a midpoint placeholder and nothing in it is attested
stops.campa: Between the marriage and the day the newly federalized capital is handed to him, twenty-six years pass in which no source consulted records a single public act: no regiment, no seat in the provincial legislature, no legation, no place on the founders' roll of the Sociedad Rural. The English article on him is a stub that jumps from a birth straight to a mayoralty. He is a landowning gentleman of the Buenos Aires elite, brother of a club president, son-in-law of a general, and for a quarter of a century the reachable record holds nothing else.
suggested_refs: A dedicated biography of Torcuato de Alvear, not located in any reachable source

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the city cut out of the province
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the verified pool; month and day unknown and defaulted to January 1. Standard accounts date the federalization law to September 1880
stops.campa: The long quarrel between the province and the nation ends in the city's favour and at the city's expense: Buenos Aires is cut out of the Province of Buenos Aires and made the federal capital, a city belonging to the Republic and to no province at all. The arrangement invents an office nobody has held, the government of a capital that governs no province, and it invents it for a town of cesspits under the patios, water carried by cart, and a Spanish street plan untouched since the viceroys ruled it out. Somebody now has to be given the town.
suggested_refs: The federalization of Buenos Aires as national capital, 1880

stops.name: Buenos Aires, sede municipal: president of the Comisión Municipal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He is proclaimed president of the Comisión Municipal, the delegated body that administers the capital until the law can invent something better. He is fifty-eight years old and has held no public office that any reachable source records. What he takes charge of is a colonial grid with a modern population poured into it: a market arcade splitting the main square in half, a burial ground grown by accretion into a maze, water sold from carts, and a plan of streets whose logic ended with the Spanish empire. He holds this post for two and a half years.
suggested_refs: The Comisión Municipal de Buenos Aires, 1880-1883

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: Buschiazzo is called in
stops.date_confidence: the source gives only the year 1880. Since the commission is given as head of the Comisión Municipal, which he assumed on 4 December 1880, the day here is a placeholder inside that month and is not attested
stops.campa: He calls in Juan Antonio Buschiazzo, Italian-born, municipal architect, and hands him the Recoleta: the field behind the Franciscan convent where the city has buried its dead since 1822, ungated, unpaved, grown crooked by accretion. The instruction is to make a necropolis of it, a city of the dead laid out the way a city is laid out, with streets that go somewhere and a front door that means something. Alvear is fifty-eight. The ground he is ordering surveyed is the ground he will be carried into ten years from now.
suggested_refs: Juan Antonio Buschiazzo, municipal architect of Buenos Aires

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the wall, the paved streets, the portico
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the date plaque at the entrance; month and day unknown and defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: The work is done. A brick wall closes the ground; the internal streets are paved and given lines; a portico of four Greek Doric columns stands at the entrance, Requiescant in pace cut on the outer face and Expectamus Dominum on the inner, with eleven allegorical figures around them. The plaque by the gate carries three dates, 1822 for the founding, 1881 for this renovation, and a third for a renovation a century off. From here the vaults rise along avenues, and every general, president and heiress buried afterward is buried inside a plan.
stops.quote: One of the great services owed to the superior direction of the Municipality, of the Intendente Don Torcuato de Alvear, is the complete transformation of that neighborhood.
stops.quote_source: Santiago Calzadilla, Las Beldades de mi Tiempo, chapter XV (Buenos Aires, 1891; 1919 edition digitized at es.wikisource.org). Own translation from the Spanish
suggested_refs: The neoclassical portico of the Cementerio de la Recoleta, 1881
Santiago Calzadilla, Las Beldades de mi Tiempo (1891)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the future line of the avenue: the petition to Irigoyen
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown and defaulted to a placeholder early in the year
stops.campa: He goes to Bernardo de Irigoyen, Minister of the Interior, with a proposal the capital has no power to execute by itself: one wide avenue driven west from the Plaza de Mayo through the middle of the colonial blocks, in imitation of Madrid and Paris. He does not ask for money. He asks for a declaration of public utility, the instrument that lets a government take a man's house and pay him for it afterward. Nothing can be cut until the Congress agrees the cut is public. What he is requesting is permission to open his own city with a knife.
suggested_refs: Bernardo de Irigoyen, Minister of the Interior, and the 1882 public-utility petition

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Åberg government house: Roca appoints him
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The venue is uncertain: in May 1883 there was no unified Casa de Gobierno, only Åberg's government house of 1882 and Kihlberg's post office of 1878 standing separately, joined by Tamburini's arch from 1884 and completed only in 1898
stops.campa: The Ley Orgánica of 1882 creates the office. President Julio Argentino Roca fills it with him, and he becomes the first intendente municipal of Buenos Aires: appointed, not elected, answerable to the president who federalized the city and then built the post. There is as yet no single government house to receive him. Åberg's building of 1882 and Kihlberg's post office of 1878 stand apart on the same ground, and the arch that will join them into one rose-coloured house is a year from being begun. He has four years, and the law says so.
suggested_refs: The Ley Orgánica de la Municipalidad, 1882
The Åberg government house and the Kihlberg post office before the 1884 unification

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo: the Recova Vieja, the central arch
stops.date_confidence: attested: the central arch was demolished from 9 August 1883, the work lasting eight days, by order of the intendente. The frequently repeated date of 25 May 1883 is wrong and is not used
stops.campa: The picks go into the Recova Vieja, the arcaded market built between 1802 and 1804 to Juan Bautista Segismundo's design, which for eighty years has stood across the middle of the square dividing the Plaza de la Victoria from the Plaza 25 de Mayo. The central arch takes eight days to come down. When the dust settles the two squares are one square, open from the Cabildo to the river, and the city can see its own government from one end of the ground to the other. The wings are still standing. They belong to the Anchorena.
suggested_refs: The Recova Vieja of Juan Bautista Segismundo, 1802-1804

stops.name: Hospital San Roque, Urquiza 609: the delayed hospital opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The Hospital San Roque is inaugurated at Urquiza 609 in Balvanera, the building Buschiazzo's, the ground a set of provisional pavilions thrown up during the cholera of 1868 and never replaced since. The record calls it simply the delayed hospital; the delay has run fifteen years. In 1914, after the death of the physician José María Ramos Mejía, it takes his name and keeps it. The month that clears the arcade off the Plaza de Mayo also opens a hospital four kilometres west of the square, on the far side of the town he has just been given.
suggested_refs: Hospital General de Agudos José María Ramos Mejía, Urquiza 609

stops.name: Paseo de la Recoleta: the promenade on the barranca
stops.date_confidence: year attributed to his tenure by the source; no founding date is given, and month and day are defaulted to January 1. The coordinate is the modern Plaza Intendente Alvear
stops.campa: Above the cemetery wall, on the barranca where the river once broke, he lays out a formal promenade: gravelled walks, plantings, benches, the ground between the Franciscan convent and the bluff turned into a place where the city walks on a Sunday instead of merely burying. Recoleta until now is a convent, a graveyard, and open country behind them. From this promenade the whole quarter takes the shape the mansions will come to face, and the walks are laid out for a public that has not yet moved up the hill. Within ten years the plaza will carry his name.
suggested_refs: The Paseo de la Recoleta, later Plaza Intendente Alvear

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo: the Anchorena wings come down
stops.date_confidence: attested: the remaining wings, in Anchorena ownership, were demolished between 8 and 14 May 1884, once the expropriation had concluded
stops.campa: The expropriation concludes and the last of the recova falls in a week, the Anchorena paid, the final colonial arcade off the Plaza de Mayo gone. The square becomes what it has been ever since: one continuous ground running from the Cabildo to the government house, where a crowd can stand undivided and be counted from a balcony. Every gathering the country will hold there is held on a floor an intendente cleared in two campaigns, the first in August with picks and the second in May with lawyers, nine months apart.
suggested_refs: The Anchorena expropriation and the final demolition of the Recova, May 1884

segments.name: The Avenue Cut Through the Colonial Grid (1884-1894)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the line of the avenue: Law 1,583
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the verified pool; some standard accounts date the law to 16 October 1884, and the discrepancy is left standing
stops.campa: National Law 1,583 authorizes the opening of an avenue not less than thirty metres wide, running from the Plaza de Mayo west to the ground where the Congress will one day stand. It is what he asked Irigoyen for in 1882, arriving as statute. One hundred and fifteen properties lie in the line. Of those, eighty-five are in the end given up by their owners in exchange for exemption from municipal tax, which is to say the capital buys its boulevard with forgiveness instead of cash. The avenue is to be cut through the blocks, not routed around them.
suggested_refs: National Law 1,583 of 1884, authorizing the Avenida de Mayo

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo: the Cabildo cut back
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The oldest public buildings on the Plaza de Mayo go under the picks: the Casa de Policía, and a part of the Cabildo itself, the viceroys' town hall where the Republic was declared, cut back to widen the mouth of the avenue. Alvear has been a year out of office and has two years to live; the picks are swung by a municipality he no longer runs. The statute he obtained eats the building where the country began, and nobody stops them. The city has decided which of the two it needs.
suggested_refs: The truncation of the Cabildo de Buenos Aires for the Avenida de Mayo

stops.name: Avenida de Mayo: the boulevard opened
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, under intendente Federico Pinedo, whose term ran 20 June 1893 to 20 August 1894
stops.campa: The Avenida de Mayo is opened, twelve years after the petition to Irigoyen and four years after the death of the man who wrote it, under the intendente Federico Pinedo. It runs thirty metres wide from the government house to the Congress, and along it the city proceeds to build the Europe it has been describing to itself: mansard roofs, Spanish tiles, cupolas, cafés with mirrors. It becomes the street the country walks down. Alvear's name is on none of it, and he never saw it opened.
suggested_refs: The inauguration of the Avenida de Mayo, 9 July 1894

segments.name: The Registry, the Parks, and the Water (1884-1887)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, sede municipal: the Registro Civil
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the Spanish article on him; month and day unknown and defaulted to January 1. Direct verification of a dedicated article on the city's civil registry failed with a 404, so the year is reported rather than independently corroborated
stops.campa: The Municipality opens a Registro Civil for the capital, on the counsel of Dr Guillermo Rawson: births, marriages and deaths recorded by the city rather than by the parish. From this year a person in Buenos Aires exists first in a municipal book and only afterward in a baptismal one, and the city can count what it governs. The record of the man who signs it into being is itself thin: nobody registered Torcuato de Alvear's own first thirty years anywhere the searches can reach.
suggested_refs: Guillermo Rawson and the Registro Civil of the city of Buenos Aires

stops.name: Parque Agronómico: green ground west of the built city
stops.date_confidence: no founding date is given by any source; the year is a placeholder inside the 1883-1887 term. The coordinate is the later Facultad de Agronomía, and the identification is plausible only: that faculty traces its own site to a 1901 authorization and a 1904 institute and names no park of the 1880s
stops.campa: Among the green spaces credited to his intendencia is a Parque Agronómico on the open ground west of the built city, out past the Chacarita lands where the town gives way to fields and the cattle roads. The identification of that ground with the later Facultad de Agronomía is plausible and no more; the faculty dates its own site from a 1901 authorization and names no park of the previous century. What is attested is the policy: a capital taking green ground by decree, west of the built blocks, while that land is still cheap.
suggested_refs: The lands of the Chacarita de los Colegiales and the later Facultad de Agronomía

stops.name: Parque de la Convalecencia: the park south of the city
stops.date_confidence: no founding date is given by any source; the year is a placeholder inside the term. The coordinate is approximate, marking the southern Convalecencia hospital lands: the common identification of this park with the Parque Rivadavia in Caballito is false, and there is no clean modern equivalent to place it on
stops.campa: South of the built city, on the Convalecencia lands where the hospices stand, another of the intendencia's parks is opened. The name is nearly all that survives of it. It is often identified with the Parque Rivadavia in Caballito, and that is wrong: the Caballito ground was the Lezica family's quinta, expropriated after 1908 and made a plaza only in 1928. The Convalecencia park belongs to the southern hospital lands and has no clean modern successor, an act of his government whose exact site the city has since mislaid.
suggested_refs: The Convalecencia lands and the later Hospicio de las Mercedes, south Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the flags of the British invasions, framed
stops.date_confidence: no date whatever is given. Calzadilla's memoir was published in 1891 and speaks of the framing as accomplished under Alvear's administration, so the date here is a placeholder inside the 1883-1887 term and is not attested
stops.campa: In the municipal keeping are the colours taken from the British regiments in the invasions of 1806 and 1807, among them the flag of the 71st of the line, trophies eighty years old and handled until now like so much bunting. Under his administration they are mounted in frames and kept properly. He is pulling down the arcade the viceroys built and putting the cloth stripped off the British behind glass. A chronicler writing the year after his death remembers him by name for the frames.
stops.quote: Its flags, among them that of the 71st infantry line, are today kept placed in luxurious frames, thanks to the Intendente Don Torcuato Alvear.
stops.quote_source: Santiago Calzadilla, Las Beldades de mi Tiempo, chapter V (Buenos Aires, 1891; 1919 edition digitized at es.wikisource.org). Own translation from the Spanish
suggested_refs: The captured colours of the British invasions of 1806-1807 in municipal keeping

stops.name: Recoleta, the Establecimiento de Aguas Corrientes: mains, paving, light
stops.date_confidence: the source is general and gives no single dated event; the year is a placeholder inside the 1883-1887 term. The coordinate is the period waterworks at Recoleta, taken as the nearest identifiable landmark and approximate
stops.campa: The unglamorous half of the work has no ceremony and no single date: piped water pushed out along the streets from the Recoleta works, paving carried past the edge of the old built-up grid, gas and then electric light on the corners, the tramways and the lighting of the public roads improved together. A city of cesspits and carted water becomes a city with mains. None of it is quotable. The town buried its cholera dead within living memory, and this is the work that decides whether it buries them again.
suggested_refs: The Establecimiento de Aguas Corrientes at Recoleta

stops.name: Buenos Aires, sede municipal: the boundary pushed into the province
stops.date_confidence: the enlargement is placed in his tenure by the Spanish article, which gives no day; month and day are defaulted to January 1 and the year is the last of his term
stops.campa: The municipal territory is enlarged, taking in land that until now belongs to the Province of Buenos Aires, and a boundary is drawn around the capital far wider than the city that fills it. Nothing marks the line on the ground. It is a survey and a decree, an argument won on paper seven years after the federalization. Half a century later the line is built: from late 1936 the Avenida General Paz is laid along it, a motorway tracing a decision taken by a municipal government while he sat at the head of it.
suggested_refs: The 1887 enlargement of the federal capital and the later Avenida General Paz

segments.name: The Term Ends and the Sea (1887-1890)

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the four years run out
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, four years to the day from the appointment
stops.campa: Four years to the day from his appointment, the term fixed by law runs out and he lays the office down. He is sixty-five. The town handed to him four years ago had a colonial market standing across the middle of its main square and a colonial street plan behind it; neither is there now. The avenue he obtained by statute will not be opened for another seven years, and the parks, the mains and the walled cemetery are already on the ground. Every intendente after him inherits a capital cut open.
suggested_refs: The four-year term of the first intendencia, 10 May 1883 to 10 May 1887

stops.name: Buenos Aires: Antonio F. Crespo takes the office
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Antonio F. Crespo is installed as intendente four days later, the second man to hold the post. Nothing about the succession is remarkable. The office has survived its founder. From here the capital has a mayor as a matter of course, appointed by the president, sitting in the same rooms, spending on the same works. Alvear walks out of the municipality and into a silence as complete as the one before 1880. What he did with the next three and a half years, no source consulted records.
suggested_refs: Antonio F. Crespo, second intendente of Buenos Aires

stops.name: Paris: the voyage to Europe
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. One source says only that he died on a return voyage from Europe; no port of departure, ship, itinerary or destination is recoverable. Paris stands here as the conventional destination of such a voyage and is attested for him by nothing; the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: Late in life he goes to Europe. Nothing of the itinerary survives, not a port of departure nor a ship's name nor a city: the single source that mentions the voyage at all mentions it only to explain where he was when he died. Paris stands here for the whole of it, because Paris is where a Buenos Aires gentleman of his fortune and generation goes, and because Paris is one of the two cities he had asked the Congress for leave to copy into the middle of his own. He is sixty-eight years old, and at some point in that year he starts home.
suggested_refs: The unrecorded European voyage of 1890

stops.name: South Atlantic, off the Río de la Plata: death at sea by one account
stops.date_confidence: the date is agreed by all sources; the place is not. This stop follows the account in the Avenida de Mayo article, which has him die on the return voyage from Europe. No ship and no position are given, and the coordinate is a notional point on a plausible track, not a documented one
stops.campa: By one account the end comes at sea. The article on his avenue states plainly that he died during the return voyage from Europe on the eighth of December 1890, which would put the death somewhere off the mouth of the Plata, a few days' steaming from the city he had rebuilt, with the coast not yet in sight. No ship is named and no position given. The date is the one thing every source agrees on, and it is the same date under either version of where he was standing when it arrived.
suggested_refs: The South Atlantic packet route from Europe to the Río de la Plata, 1890

stops.name: Buenos Aires: death in the city by the other account
stops.date_confidence: attested date; the place contradicts the preceding stop. The English article says he died in Buenos Aires, the Spanish article on him gives the year with no place, and the article on his avenue puts him at sea. The contradiction is left standing rather than resolved
stops.campa: By the other account, the commoner one, he dies in Buenos Aires at sixty-eight. The English article on him says so; the Spanish article on him gives the year and no place at all; only the account of his avenue puts him on a ship. Nothing reachable settles it and the two versions are left standing side by side. Either way the date is the eighth of December 1890, four years before the Avenida de Mayo is opened, and either way he is carried up the slope to the Recoleta and in through a gate that he built.
suggested_refs: The conflicting death notices of December 1890

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: buried inside his own plan
stops.date_confidence: no source consulted gives the day of the burial; the date here is a placeholder set the day after the attested death and is not attested
stops.campa: He is buried in the Cementerio de la Recoleta: in through the Doric portico he commissioned, along the paved avenues he had ordered surveyed, past the brick wall that closed the ground, into a family plot. The man who turned the necropolis into a plan is filed inside the plan. No source consulted names the day. The vault that will hold him properly is not built and will not be for fifteen years; for now he lies where his own survey put the streets, nine years after he sent Buschiazzo up the hill to draw them.
suggested_refs: The Alvear plot at the Cementerio de la Recoleta before the 1905 mausoleum

stops.name: Plaza Intendente Alvear: the promenade takes his name
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no day is given, and since the renaming follows his death on 8 December the date here is a placeholder at the end of that year
stops.campa: The Municipality gives the promenade above the cemetery his name. The Paseo de la Recoleta, the walks and plantings he laid out on the barranca in the first year of his intendencia, becomes the Plaza Intendente Alvear and keeps that name. It is the office naming ground after the first man to hold it, within weeks of his death. The quarter around it is by now filling with the houses of the families who will use the cemetery below, and the avenue that runs past their doors will carry the family name as well.
suggested_refs: Plaza Intendente Alvear, Recoleta

stops.name: Plaza Intendente Alvear: the monument of 1900
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown and defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: A monument goes up on the plaza: a Doric column of Carrara marble carrying a bronze Glory, with a bust of the intendente below, by the sculptors A. Jons and Juan Lauer. Three reliefs are set into the stone, and they name exactly what the city decided to remember of him ten years after his death: the opening of the Avenida de Mayo, the paving of the streets, and the works at the Recoleta. The avenue in the relief has been open six years by the day the column is unveiled. He never walked a metre of it.

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the Christophersen mausoleum
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown and defaulted to January 1. The date and circumstances of the transfer of Carlos María de Alvear's remains from New York are given by no source consulted
stops.campa: A family mausoleum is raised inside the cemetery, designed by Alejandro Christophersen, and the Alvear dead are gathered into it. Carlos María de Alvear, minister in New York, dead there in 1852, comes home to this vault; when and by what ship, no source consulted says. Father and son lie in the one chamber: the Director Supremo who was thrown out of the country he helped make, and the son who spent four years remaking its capital and is by now fifteen years dead in the ground he had ordered walled, paved and gated.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the son takes the presidency
stops.date_confidence: the verified pool gives the presidency as 1922-1928 without a day; month and day are defaulted to January 1. Standard accounts date the inauguration to October 1922
stops.campa: Marcelo Torcuato de Alvear takes the presidency of the Republic. He is the son born in Buenos Aires in 1868, and he governs for six years from a house at the head of the square his father cleared, at the mouth of the avenue his father cut. Three men of the name pass through that one square: the Director Supremo of 1815 who was driven out of it, the intendente who levelled the arcade across it, and the president who walks out onto the balcony above it. The city keeps the middle one under a marble column, on a plaza named for the office he was the first to hold.
